title: Remove Outermost Parentheses
description: Brute force to optimized: splitting into primitive pieces first versus a single-pass depth counter that decides inclusion directly per character.

blocks.text: A valid parentheses string is "primitive" if it is non-empty, and cannot be split into two smaller non-empty valid parentheses strings. Given a valid parentheses string s, it can always be uniquely decomposed into a sequence of primitive valid parentheses strings placed one after another. Return s after removing the OUTERMOST pair of parentheses from every one of these primitive pieces.

blocks.caption: A running nesting depth counter reveals exactly which parentheses are "outermost" for their primitive piece: skip those, keep everything else

blocks.text: The string first needs to be understood as a sequence of independent, self-contained balanced pieces (each one's nesting depth starts and ends at 0, never touching 0 in between); within EACH piece, only its own single outermost opening and closing parenthesis should be removed, keeping everything else (including any inner nested parentheses) intact.

blocks.title: Analogy: Removing the Outer Envelope From Each Separately Mailed Letter
blocks.text: Imagine several letters, each sealed in its own separate outer envelope, placed one after another in a single stack of mail. This problem asks to remove just the OUTER envelope from each individual letter (keeping any inner folders or smaller envelopes inside each letter completely intact), then restack all the now-unwrapped letters back together in their original order.

blocks.caption: A depth transition from 0 to 1 marks an outermost opening parenthesis; a transition from 1 to 0 marks an outermost closing parenthesis, both skipped

blocks.text: Before explicitly splitting the string into its primitive pieces and then stripping each one's outer characters separately, notice that a SINGLE running depth counter directly identifies exactly which characters are "outermost" for their piece, without ever needing to materialize the pieces at all.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: An opening parenthesis encountered while the current depth is 0 is, BY DEFINITION, the start of a new primitive piece: it is that piece's own outermost open, and should be skipped.

Observation 2: A closing parenthesis that brings the depth BACK DOWN to 0 is, by definition, the end of that primitive piece: it is that piece's own outermost close, and should also be skipped.

Observation 3: Every OTHER parenthesis (opened or closed while depth is already greater than the relevant threshold) is an INNER character of its piece, and must be kept exactly as-is.

Observation 4: This means a single pass, incrementing/decrementing a depth counter and checking its value at each step (BEFORE incrementing for opens, AFTER decrementing for closes), directly identifies and skips exactly the right characters, without ever needing to actually split the string into separate primitive pieces first.
This is a single-pass depth-tracking technique: the depth counter itself reveals exactly which characters are each primitive piece's own outermost pair, without materializing the pieces at all.

First explicitly split the string into its primitive pieces (each ending exactly where a running depth counter returns to 0), then strip each piece's own first and last character (its outermost pair) and concatenate the results.

items: Walk through the string, tracking a running depth counter; whenever it returns to 0, the substring since the last split point is one complete primitive piece.
For each primitive piece, strip its first and last character (the outermost pair), then concatenate all the stripped pieces together.

codes.python:
def remove_outer_parentheses(s):
    primitives = []                                                        # split s into its primitive (balanced, non-empty) pieces first
    depth = 0
    start = 0
    for i, c in enumerate(s):
        depth += 1 if c == '(' else -1
        if depth == 0:                                                     # a primitive piece ends exactly when depth returns to 0
            primitives.append(s[start:i + 1])
            start = i + 1
    return ''.join(p[1:-1] for p in primitives)                            # strip each primitive's own outermost pair of parentheses


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(remove_outer_parentheses("(()())(())"))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A primitive piece is precisely identified by tracking where the running depth counter returns to exactly 0, which is the formal definition given in the problem.
Explicitly materializing each piece as its own substring makes stripping its outer pair straightforward (simply substring[1:-1]).

blocks.text: Correctly identifies every primitive piece and strips exactly its outermost pair, following the problem's definition directly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass to split plus a linear amount of work to strip and rejoin.
Space: O(n), for the list of primitive substrings.

Limitation: explicitly materializing each primitive piece as a separate substring is unnecessary overhead; the SAME depth counter can directly decide, character by character, whether to include it in the final result, without ever forming intermediate substrings.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force splits into substrings first, then strips each one. Instead, track the SAME depth counter directly against the final result: for an opening parenthesis, include it only if depth is ALREADY greater than 0 (meaning it is NOT this piece's outermost open), then increment depth; for a closing parenthesis, decrement depth first, then include it only if depth is STILL greater than 0 (meaning it was NOT this piece's outermost close).

Walk through the string once with a running depth counter. For "(": if depth > 0, append it to the result; then increment depth. For ")": decrement depth first; then if depth > 0, append it to the result.
Track a single running depth counter directly against the final result, skipping exactly the outermost open/close of each primitive piece.

blocks.text: The included characters form "()()" + "()" = "()()()", matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the result string (excluding this, O(1) extra beyond the output).

The depth counter's value at the exact moment each character is processed directly reveals whether that character is an outermost boundary of its primitive piece. An opening parenthesis is outermost exactly when depth was 0 just before it (the very start of a new piece); a closing parenthesis is outermost exactly when depth becomes 0 immediately after it (the very end of a piece). Checking these conditions with the correct ordering (check-then-increment for opens, decrement-then-check for closes) correctly identifies and skips exactly those two characters per piece.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["An opening parenthesis when depth == 0","This is a piece's outermost open: skip it, then increment depth"],["An opening parenthesis when depth > 0","This is an inner character: include it, then increment depth"],["A closing parenthesis that brings depth back to 0","This is a piece's outermost close: decrement depth, then skip it (since depth is now 0)"]]}

items: For opening parentheses, the depth check happens BEFORE incrementing, since the relevant question is "was I already inside a piece before this character?"
For closing parentheses, the depth check happens AFTER decrementing, since the relevant question is "does this character bring me back down to the piece's baseline (0)?"
This asymmetric ordering (check-then-increment vs. decrement-then-check) is the subtle detail that makes the single-pass approach correct without ever materializing substrings.

blocks.text: A running nesting-depth counter, tracked directly against a single pass over the string, can identify structural boundaries (like "outermost" characters of independent balanced pieces) without ever needing to explicitly split the string into those pieces first.

items: Getting the check/increment (or decrement/check) ORDER backward for opens versus closes, which subtly breaks the correctness of exactly which characters get skipped.
Explicitly splitting into primitive substrings first when the single-pass version achieves the identical result more directly.
Forgetting that MULTIPLE primitive pieces can exist back-to-back in the same string, each needing its own outermost pair removed independently.

items: Explicitly explaining WHY the check happens before incrementing for opens but after decrementing for closes (the asymmetry is intentional and meaningful) demonstrates precise understanding rather than just memorized code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove the OUTERMOST layer from each independent/primitive balanced piece" points toward tracking a running nesting depth counter directly against the final result, in a single pass.

items: How would you instead COUNT the number of primitive pieces, rather than stripping them? Simply count how many times the depth counter returns to exactly 0.
How would you find the MAXIMUM nesting depth reached anywhere in the string? Track the running maximum of the depth counter throughout the same single pass.

How does this connect to Score of Parentheses, which also tracks nesting depth? Both rely on the SAME core insight: a running depth counter directly reveals structural properties of nested balanced parentheses without needing to explicitly parse a tree.

The "track nesting depth directly against the output" technique, shared conceptually with Score of Parentheses elsewhere in this category, both avoiding an explicit parse tree in favor of a single running counter.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space (intermediate substrings).
Optimized (single-pass depth tracking): O(n) time, O(n) output space only.

items: Pattern: Single-pass nesting-depth tracking
Core Idea: A running depth counter directly reveals each primitive piece's outermost open (depth was 0 before it) and outermost close (depth becomes 0 after it), both skipped; everything else is kept
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n) (output only)
Most Important Observation: The check/increment order must be asymmetric: check-then-increment for opens, decrement-then-check for closes
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: "(": include if depth>0, then depth++. ")": depth--, then include if depth>0
